facts.statement: Amphicotylus lived during the Tithonian stage of the Late Jurassic in Colorado, Wyoming, and Oklahoma.
facts.quote: Amphicotylus is an extinct genus of goniopholidid mesoeucrocodylian from the Tithonian of Colorado, Wyoming, and Oklahoma.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope described Amphicotylus in 1878 using dorsal and lumbar vertebrae, ribs, and osteoderms.
facts.quote: Amphicotylus was first described by Edward Drinker Cope in 1878 based on dorsal and lumbar vertebrae, ribs and osteoderms.

facts.statement: Cope named the type species A. lucasii after Superintendent Lucas and estimated the animal was smaller than the modern American Alligator.
facts.quote: Cope determined the animal to have been smaller than the extant American Alligator and named the species A. lucasii after Superintendent Lucas who initially made the discovery.

facts.statement: Excavations in 1993 at the East Camarasaurus Quarry in Wyoming produced the largest and most complete goniopholidid skeleton known.
facts.quote: Excavations in the East Camarasaurus Quarry, Wyoming, in 1993 yielded the largest and most complete goniopholidid skeleton found to date.

facts.statement: Amphicotylus possessed a roughly triangular, platyrostral skull shape similar to modern crocodilians.
facts.quote: Amphicotylus had a roughly triangular, platyrostral skull similar in shape to that of modern crocodilians.

facts.statement: Amphicotylus is distinguished from Goniopholis by having palatines completely separated by the choana.
facts.quote: In members of Amphicotylus, the palatines are completely separated from one another by the choana while in Goniopholis the palatines make broad contact prior to the choana.

facts.statement: The hyoid apparatus morphology suggests A. milesi could raise the ventral fold of the gular valve to separate narial and oral passages.
facts.quote: Based on the morphology of the hyoid apparatus and its muscle attachments, A. milesi would have been able to raise the ventral fold of the gullar valve, separating narial and oral passages.

facts.statement: This adaptation allowed Amphicotylus to open its mouth underwater while breathing, provided its nostrils remained above the surface.
facts.quote: This adaptation for semi-aquatic life would have allowed Amphicotylus and other Neosuchians to completely cut out the oral cavity from respiration, giving it the ability to open its mouth underwater while continuing to breathe as long as the nares are above the surface.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic studies consistently place Amphicotylus deep within Goniopholididae, just outside the clade containing most European members.
facts.quote: Studies have repeatedly found Amphicotylus to be nested deep within Goniopholididae, typically located just outside the clade that contains most European members of the group.

facts.statement: There is a debate regarding the relationship of Denazinosuchus to Amphicotylus, with some studies viewing it as a sister taxon and others placing it in the European clade.
facts.quote: Denazinosuchus, a late Cretaceous member of Goniopholididae, was recovered as a sister taxon to Amphicotylus by Puértolas-Pascual et al. 2015, but as part of the "European clade" by Yoshida et al. 2021.

facts.statement: Amphicotylus lived from the Kimmeridgian to the Tithonian, between 152.21 and 143.1 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Kimmeridgian to Tithonian (152.21 to 143.1 million years ago)
